entries.title: White Sox hitting director Ryan Fuller talks offensive improvement, and the development that remains
entries.summary: <p>In his second season, White Sox hitting director Ryan Fuller expected the offense to be improved.</p><p>He would not have promised the highest-scoring unit (4.74 runs per game entering Wednesday) in the American League, even when hitting coach Derek Shomon was foretelling top-10 production in spring</p><p>“At the time, it was man, we’ve got a ton of talent, but it's going to be a lot of things coming together the right way to achieve that,” Fuller told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Fuller refers to Shomon, assistant hitting coach Joel McKeithan and major league assistant Tony Medina as the “boots on the ground,” rallying Sox hitters through day-to-day challenges, and reinforcing larger initiatives. Broadly, the White Sox are scoring more this year because they are hitting for more power than anticipated.</p><p>Colson Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Miguel Vargas all posting 30-homer campaigns lead an offense that is sixth in MLB in home runs, and looks primed to clear the 200-homer threshold for the first time since 2012. The raw pop of Murakami and Montgomery was previously established. For others, it had to be developed.</p><p>“Last year, 30th in bat speed; we don't want to be last in any meaningful category, so obviously that was a focus,” Fuller told the Sun-Times. “It's the fifth highest year-over-year bat speed increase in the big leagues, so a lot to be proud of.”</p><p>With Chase Meidroth, Sam Antonacci, and Vargas being the largest beneficiary, Fuller says the increased capacity for hard contact is three-pronged. Vargas is also the best example of a player that was challenged to add strength and explosiveness in their offseason training, and Fuller credited the coaching staff and biomechanists for cleaning out swing inefficiencies. But the most prominent addition is a regimen of weighted bat training, using branded equipment from renowned private training facility Driveline, a practice mirrored throughout their minor league system.</p><p>Though developing power provided the biggest White Sox’ offensive gains, Fuller extols the importance of contact-oriented hitters like Meidroth and Antonacci for balancing out the lineup on nights where home runs don’t come. Unlike some analysts, Fuller values a pesky two-strike approach and swing, after hunting for damage early in the count. And the Sox wouldn’t hit at all if they weren’t utilizing simulated at-bats off their Trajekt machine to chase out of the zone less than any point of their recorded history.</p><p>Some of the White Sox offensive identity is simply personnel. They have the fourth-lowest contact rate in the league because their roster is full of loose movers, long levers and uphill swing paths. Their runs come in huge chunks, as do the whiffs and inconsistency, especially with the roster’s youth.</p><p>“It's not like we're the Dodgers, where guys have been in the league for five-plus years, and you really understand their profiles,” Fuller said. “The adjustments they're going to make, understanding how pitchers are attacking them better. We believe that those are going to get to a spot where they're going to be stable.”</p><p>That extends to the White Sox’ currently most embattled hitter and for most of the year, their biggest revelation in Murakami. On Wednesday, Murakami’s brutal slump took another bleak turn, as his streak of consecutive plate appearances with a strikeout reached eight until he was hit by a pitch in the sixth.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/03/white-sox-keeping-luis-castillo-in-rotation-and-munetaka-murakami-high-in-batting-order-amid-struggles-will-venable-astros-road-trip-zach-bove-al-central-division-playoffs" target="_blank" ><u>Murakami said in Houston</u></a> that he felt his swing path had become too uphill, requiring his timing and pitch selection to be letter-perfect to make contact. Fuller echoed those sentiments, saying the first baseman’s batting cage work is focused on returning to the baselines of his All-Star caliber start. That he and Sox hitters are ahead of schedule, never assured that there wasn’t more work to do.</p><p>“If it were any other rookie, we would be saying it’s part of the learning experience,” Fuller said. “For these guys to be as successful as they have been in their early part of their careers, learning lessons, making adjustments, and then coming back productive, that's the goal.”</p>

entries.title: Des Plaines police officer fatally shoots man while responding to domestic disturbance
entries.summary: <p>A man died after a Des Plaines police officer shot him during a response to a domestic dispute, according to police.</p><p>Officers were responding to a “domestic disturbance” at a home in the 2000 block of Touhy Avenue at 2:32 p.m. when an officer shot Ayham Babidi, 21, during the encounter, police said. No other details about the shooting were released.</p><p>Babidi was taken to a local hospital where he later died, according to police. The Des Plaines Major Case Assistance Team is investigating.</p>

entries.title: Kevin Gausman gives up three homers, and Cubs’ starting staff stays inconsistent heading toward October
entries.summary: <p>MILWAUKEE – Are <b>Jed Hoyer</b>’s worst fears coming true?</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ team president <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/01/cubs-home-runs-record-jed-hoyer-front-office-pitching-starting-rotation-playoffs-postseason-shota-imanaga-matthew-boyd" >cited an inconsistent pitching staff as a concern</a> during his most recent meeting with the media, and a week later, he hasn’t been given any reason to think those issues have been ironed out.</p><p>“The position-playing group, we’re the No. 1 offense, No. 1 defense right now. That’s wonderful. Obviously, that’s the backbone of our team,” Hoyer said last week. “There’s no question of what our strength is. [But] we do need to get consistent starting pitching, throw strikes consistently and hopefully let the position players do the work.”</p><p>While a stumbling bullpen is generating the most fan complaints, it was starter <b>Kevin Gausman</b> – imported by Hoyer’s front office at the trade deadline to be a top-of-the-rotation arm – who was knocked around by the Brewers on Wednesday, crushed for three homers and seven runs in his briefest outing as a Cub to date.</p><p>A night after lefty <b>David Peterson</b> didn’t make it out of the fifth inning, Gausman lasted just four innings, his third Cubs start not to make it to a 15th out.</p><p>Gausman has gone back and forth between looking capable of starting (and dominating) Game 1 of a playoff series and getting hit around.</p><p>In other words, he’s been inconsistent, adding fuel to Hoyer’s nightmares that a hit-or-miss pitching staff could help sink the Cubs in the playoffs.</p><p>Though lefty <b>Shota Imanaga</b> has received season-long attention for surrendering long balls – he entered Wednesday still leading the majors with 33 home runs given up – Gausman has been taken deep plenty since coming to the Cubs in a trade at the beginning of last month, now with nine homers on his tab in seven starts.</p><p>Hoyer spent big, in terms of prospects, at the deadline to net Gausman and fellow right-hander <b>Clay Holmes</b>, whose worst outing as a Cub came Sunday, when he allowed a career-worst eight runs and didn’t make it out of the fifth inning.</p><p>Gausman has now had three starts in a Cubs uniform allowing at least five runs, the sort of thing that can tank a playoff game – and a season, along with it.</p><p>That’s not what Hoyer envisioned, obviously, and though Gausman and Holmes – who pitched in the two most recent World Series, respectively – have the experience and ability to straighten things out, that inconsistency is evidently worth fretting about for the guy running the show.</p><p>On top of it all, this wasn’t some random team on the other end of a bad outing. These Brewers are the team that have owned the NL Central, eliminated the Cubs from the playoffs last year and figure to stand in their way again this October.</p><p>If the Cubs are going to clear the Brewers-shaped hurdle in front of them, they need what Hoyer said they need: more consistency from their arms.</p><p><b>Helping Happ heal</b></p><p>Left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b> was in the Cubs’ lineup Wednesday a day after fouling a pitch off his foot the night before, serving as the DH instead of playing the outfield.</p><p>“It’s a little sore today,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “He didn’t feel great cutting and things like that, so we’ll try to minimize the impact and the exposure to it with the DH.”</p><p><b>Surgery for Maton</b></p><p>Counsell relayed that righty reliever <b>Phil Maton</b> will have surgery on his ailing knee later this week.</p><p>The Cubs inked Maton to a two-year free-agent deal in the offseason, but bedeviled by the knee injury throughout the summer, he was ineffective when on the mound, the owner of a 6.18 ERA.</p>

entries.title: Police investigating death of woman pulled from Little Calumet River
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are investigating after a woman was pulled from the Little Calumet River in West Pullman Wednesday morning and later died, according to the department.</p><p>Ralphealle Howard, 26, was pulled out of the water in the 13000 block of South Indiana Avenue at 10:48 a.m., police said. She was taken to Roseland Hospital, where she later died.</p><p>Her death is under investigation.</p>

entries.title: Lincoln-Way East students walk out to denounce racism their classmates directed at Homewood-Flossmoor peers
entries.summary: <p>Dozens of students walked out of Lincoln-Way East High School in south suburban Frankfort Wednesday morning in support of students at nearby Homewood-Flossmoor High School. </p><p>The Lincoln-Way East students were protesting after two incidents of racial harassment involving their school and H-F.</p><p>The first occurred Friday when Lincoln-Way East students were caught on video racially taunting H-F students at a football game in Flossmoor by mimicking monkeys.</p><p>Then on Saturday, H-F officials said a coach and members of Lincoln-Way East’s girls cross country team racially taunted the H-F team at a meet in west suburban Western Springs.</p><p>The events prompted Lincoln-Way East students to denounce what transpired and support their peers impacted by the acts.</p><p>The mood was somber and the halls were nearly empty at Lincoln-Way East ahead of the demonstration. But the students who remained said they were determined to make their voices heard.</p><p>“We want to let people know that Lincoln-Way East is not just a predominantly white school that's full of racist people,” said 14-year-old Teniola Omokaye. “There's a big demographic of Black people that go here and we actually stand for something.”</p><p>Student organizers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/08/lincoln-way-east-racial-incident-homewood-flossmoor" >planned the walkout</a> to stand with Homewood-Flossmoor High School and send a message that the behavior does not represent the broader Lincoln-Way East student body.</p><p>Students, followed by faculty and staff, streamed out of the school chanting “Black lives matter” and “No place for racism,” as parents and community members cheered them on from across the street.</p><p></p><p></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-sports/2026/09/08/lincoln-way-east-racist-incident-homewood-flossmoor" >Second racist Lincoln-Way East incident alleged by Homewood-Flossmoor</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Lincoln-Way East acknowledged what happened at Friday’s football game and apologized. The Lincoln-Way School District, however, denied the allegations involving the girls cross-country team in a statement issued Tuesday afternoon.</p><p>In an earlier statement, H-F Supt. entries.title: 16-year-old boy fatally shot in South Loop
entries.summary: <p>A teen was fatally shot in South Loop Wednesday night, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The 16-year-old boy was found with a gunshot wound to the neck in the 1100 block of South Michigan Avenue at 9:05 p.m., police said.</p><p>He was taken to Northwestern Hospital in serious condition and later died.</p><p>No one is in custody.</p>

entries.title: Lionel Messi and Robert Lewandowski help Fire draw franchise-record crowd in 1-1 tie with Inter Miami
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fire" >Fire</a> president of business operations Dave Baldwin was busy in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fire/2026/09/08/soccer-spotlight-to-be-on-chicago-when-robert-lewandowski-and-the-fire-host-lionel-messis-inter-miami" >leadup to Wednesday’s match</a> against Lionel Messi and Inter Miami.</p><p>His phone was, too.</p><p>“There has been just a massive outpouring of support and interest,” Baldwin told the Sun-Times on Wednesday morning, hours before the Blackhawks’ Patrick Kane led the pregame Sound the Alarm tradition. “The best example I can give you is my cell phone has been ringing off the hook for the last 24 hours, from local athletes and celebrities who want to sit down by the field today.”</p><p>The celebrity players mostly delivered.</p><p>The Fire’s Robert Lewandowski scored in the 10th minute and Inter Miami’s Casemiro converted a pinpoint Messi corner kick in the 48<sup>th</sup> during the 1-1 tie. In front of a franchise-record crowd of 63,094, Messi and Lewandowski both played the full 90 minutes and showed why the Fire and Major League Soccer have invested so heavily in marquee players.</p><p>As they proved, both Messi and Lewandowski can still play despite their advanced ages.</p><p>Messi (39) started slowly but got into the match late in the first half, eventually mustering four shots on target. He did have a chance for a dramatic winner in second-half stoppage time, but his free kick hit the Fire wall. Lewandowski (38) was generally held in check, but that was after he stuck out his right leg to turn in a precise Andrew Gutman cross for his sixth goal in nine MLS games.</p><p>“The assist, it was nice to get on it, but the finish was amazing,” Gutman said. “It’s kind of easy when you just put it in a spot and [Lewandowski] does the rest.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div the game.</p><p>With Lewandowski on the roster, the Fire are averaging 41,815 in three league matches at Soldier Field. Before Lewandowski, the Fire were drawing 19,668 over eight dates.</p><p>Wednesday was Messi’s second MLS game at Soldier Field. His first appearance — a 0-0 draw on April 13, 2025 — attracted 62,538. In 2023, Messi was injured and missed the Fire’s 4-1 win, but the event still drew 62,124 after an intense team marketing campaign.</p><p>On Wednesday, Messi was still quite the attraction but not the choice of most of the fans. Unlike last year’s Chicago game between the teams, the Fire had a slight majority of the customer support, many of whom booed Messi and chanted Lewandowski’s name. Lewandowski’s applause during pregame introductions was louder than Messi’s, and Inter Miami’s pink and black or Argentina’s light blue were easy to spot but didn’t overwhelm the Fire’s red or other home team paraphernalia.</p><p>The fan response Wednesday is one example of why it made sense for the Fire to go after Lewandowski during an already-strong season. Beyond his scoring, Lewandowski’s presence has given the Fire the type of figure to draw eyeballs from around the world.</p><p>It also presents logistical challenges similar to what Miami has dealt with during the Messi era. The Fire have had to handle increased ticket demand, the need for extra security and more media requests. Those are good problems to have.</p><p>Baldwin said MLS does well to share its best practices for these obstacles during regular calls between team presidents and quarterly Board of Governors meetings.</p><p>“Thankfully, this isn’t something that caught us flat-footed, as we had been recruiting Robert for a while,” Baldwin said. “That’s really exciting. It has lived up to the hype. There are a lot of fans who are very excited for Robert and for the club to be having the success we are.”</p>
